title: Classify triangles by sides: scalene, isosceles, equilateral

lesson.title: Triangles and Their Sides

steps.say: You already know how to sort polygons by looking at their side lengths. Today we use that same skill on triangles only, and give the three kinds their real names.

visual.caption: Every triangle has three sides — the sides tell us its name

steps.say: Here is the whole idea: we count how many sides are the same length. If all three sides are different lengths, we call it scalene. If exactly two sides match, we call it isosceles. If all three sides match, we call it equilateral. That is it — just count the matching sides.

visual.caption: Seven, five and three — all different, so this one is scalene

steps.say: Look at this one. Two sides are five centimetres and five centimetres, and the bottom is four centimetres. Two sides match, so it is isosceles. The word isosceles means equal legs, like a tent with two matching poles leaning together.

Now a real worked example. Miguel is making a triangle out of licorice for a class party. He cuts pieces that are six centimetres, six centimetres and six centimetres. Let us count the matching sides. Six equals six, six equals six, so all three are the same. All three match, so this triangle is equilateral.

visual.caption: All three sides six centimetres — equilateral

steps.say: Here is a mix-up lots of kids make. Someone sees a triangle with sides of eight, eight and three centimetres and says it is scalene, because it looks stretched and pointy. But do not judge by how it looks — check the numbers. Eight and eight are the same, so two sides match, and that makes it isosceles, not scalene. Pointy or wide does not matter; only the side lengths decide.

visual.caption: It looks skinny, but two sides match — isosceles

steps.say: So remember: count the equal sides. None the same is scalene, two the same is isosceles, three the same is equilateral.

lesson.answer: Count the equal sides: zero equal is scalene, two equal is isosceles, three equal is equilateral.

practice.question: At a Vancouver park, Priya lays out three triangles with sticks. The first has sides of ten centimetres, ten centimetres and ten centimetres. The second has sides of nine centimetres, six centimetres and four centimetres. The third has sides of seven centimetres, seven centimetres and twelve centimetres. Draw a quick sketch of each if it helps, then name each triangle by its sides.
practice.answer: The first is equilateral (all three sides equal), the second is scalene (all three sides different), and the third is isosceles (two sides equal).
